docs.text: Why Galimatron ¶ Galimatron is a command line tool that keeps one versioned description of your data and lets you generate everything else from it. You describe your data once, in text files called GaL files (Galimatron Language, .gal ). Galimatron checks the description, edits it on your command, and turns it into XML . From that XML you make whatever you need: source code in the language of your choice, documentation, database schemas, test data, a web page. The model behind it is extremely simple on purpose : a few kinds of entities (aggregate, version, tag, label, ordering), and for each one a short life: it is created, changed, closed with a hash, or deleted. Entities lists all of it on one page. Simple as it is, this model is enough for about 95% of what people want to generate, and for the rest you build the missing piece from the same parts, as the dictionary in the messages example does. Key features ¶ A very simple language, and the state is only text. A GaL file looks like JSON: aggregates with versions, and tags with values. All the state of a project is in .gal files: no binaries, no database, no hidden project files. They live in git like any other text. More The history lives inside the data. Every .gal file holds all versions of a description, so a generator sees version 2 next to version 3, not only today's state. More A closed version cannot change by accident. A hash seals a version. A changed value is an error, and your XSLT cannot rewrite a sealed version: the seal moves the change into the first open one. More The Wizard edits the description for you. One command creates a version, a tag, an aggregate or a hash, and a batch of commands does many at once. You do not copy and edit many files by hand. The result is written back into the .gal files, so the project modifies itself and the next run starts from it. More The primary output is XML. Every run writes the compiled description, with the history of every version, as an ordinary XML file ( post-compiled.xml ). Running XSLT inside Galimatron is optional: Saxon, an XSLT processor, is built in and it is the convenient way, but you may read the XML with any tool, or none. More It is not tied to any language. No programming language, data format or database is built into Galimatron. You can generate anything you like. What is generated is decided by what reads the XML. More Declare once, inherit everywhere. Tags written in the root flow into every aggregate. Labels name the values and give your XSLT something to read by name. More Values that must be new in every version. A dynamic label asks your XSLT for the next id or counter, and a custom state remembers what your XSLT needs between runs. More Checked before it is written. The run parses and validates the description, and checks the seal, before your .gal files are rewritten. A failing check stops the run there. More Deterministic. The same .gal files and the same XSLT give the same result, so a run that has nothing to change leaves no diff in version control. More Easy to see what happened. A log with the time and memory of every step, a summary, and XML dumps of every stage. More Measured. Up to 500 aggregates and 100 versions, with the numbers published. The size to expect in practice, 500 aggregates and 10 versions, runs in 45 seconds to under 10 minutes, depending on the tags and the XSLT. More One tool, no library. Galimatron is one executable for Windows and Linux. You do not link it into your program. You run it, and it reads and writes the folders that you name in gal.cfg . There is an extension for Visual Studio Code. More Where Galimatron stands ¶ .gal files ──► Galimatron ──► XML (the primary output) ──► anything you like (you write) checks, edits, the full, versioned picture your XSLT, a Python script, compiles a program in any language, ... Galimatron owns the part that is hard to get right and the same for everybody: a versioned description, its checks, its edits, the history. It does not own the part that is different for every project: what to make out of it. The problem ¶ A description of data lives in many places at once. A product list sits on a wiki page. The same products are records in a database, items in the code, rows in a spreadsheet, and cases in the tests. Every copy is edited by hand, so the copies drift apart. Then the data changes. Version 2 of the list must still be understood next to version 3. Where is version 2 now? It is in a git history, or in somebody's memory. A generator that reads today's file cannot see it. Galimatron keeps the history inside the data . Every GaL file holds all versions of a description. A closed version is sealed with a hash, so it cannot change by accident. What Galimatron gives you ¶ Your problem What Galimatron does Read The same data is typed in many places. One description in GaL, compiled to XML. docs.text: Aggregates and versions ¶ The version list ¶ The root aggregate declares which versions exist. Every aggregate repeats the same list, so an aggregate can never be "at version 3" while the rest of the project is at 2. root aggregate shop { versions { 0 = { hash = '27025d7a...' }; 1 = deleted; 2 = { comment = "spring prices" }; 3; } } Declaration Meaning 3; version 3 exists and is open 0 = { hash = '...' }; version 0 is closed : a hash fixes its important values 1 = deleted; version 1 was removed. The index stays reserved. { comment = "..." } a note for people. It does not affect the data. The indexes run from 0 without gaps. Galimatron checks this on every run and tells you which aggregate breaks the rule. A version is open (you may write into it), closed (a hash is stored, read only) or deleted . See Hashes and closed versions for the closed state. What a version sees ¶ Writing a full copy of every aggregate in every version is the problem you want to avoid. A version states only its changes . What the aggregate "means" in a version is the merge of that version with everything before it. A tag written in version 0 is still there in version 1, until version 1 writes the tag again (the new value wins). delete name; removes a tag from that version on. A later version can bring the tag back by writing it. The same rule works across aggregates: the root's tags flow into every aggregate. root aggregate shop { versions { 0; 1; } } version 0 { currency = { "EUR" }; } version 1 { } aggregate apple { versions { 0; 1; } } version 0 { price = { "3" }; } version 1 { price = { "4" }; } Compiled currency price apple, version 0 EUR 3 apple, version 1 EUR 4 You wrote the currency once. A new currency in the root, in version 2, changes every aggregate in version 2 and later. Version modes ¶ Sometimes an aggregate must not take everything. A dictionary of terms may need no settings of the root. An item that was reborn may need to forget its old fields. A version mode is written before the index. version own 6 { ... } Mode Earlier versions of this aggregate Statements of the root (none) yes yes once no yes local no no own yes no The four modes, one by one ¶ The pictures below use the same data, so you can compare them. The root shop has currency in version 0 and country in version 1. The aggregate apple has price in version 0 and weight in version 1. Only the mode written before version 1 of apple changes. Each picture shows what apple ends up with in that version: green lines were inherited, struck-out lines were not. No mode. The default. The version takes everything: the earlier versions of apple and the root's tags. Nothing is lost, and this is what you want almost always. once . The version forgets what apple itself wrote before (here, price is gone), but it still receives the root's tags. Use it to start an item over while it keeps following the root. local . The version stands alone. It has nothing from the earlier versions of apple and nothing from the root, only what it writes itself. Use it for a body that must not depend on anything else. own . The version keeps what apple wrote before, and cuts itself off from the root. The root's currency and country do not reach it. Use it for an aggregate that has its own life, like a dictionary of terms that needs no settings of the root. local and own are only for aggregates. On the root they are errors. wizard create version once|local|own and wizard create aggregate once|local|own set the mode for you. A plain wizard create version keeps the mode that the previous version had: after local , the new body is a copy of the previous version's ordinary tags, so the aggregate stays self-contained. After own , the new version sees the earlier one on its own. Deleting an aggregate ¶ An aggregate that is no longer needed is not erased. A delete; in a version ends it from that version on: version 4 { delete; } The file stays. Older versions still describe it, and your XSLT can still generate the old shapes (the example with messages uses this to keep the conversion from old messages). The compiled view of version 4 and later does not have it. wizard delete aggregate name writes this delete; for you. It refuses when the aggregate is part of a closed version, because that would change a published version. With physically the file goes away, and the name can be used again. See The Wizard . Collapsing history ¶ A project that lives for years collects versions. Version 0 to version 40 may all be closed, and the new generator only needs the last one. Remove them from the file without losing the current meaning: wizard collapse version 1-4; Versions 1 to 4 are marked deleted. Their hashes and bodies go. The last value of each tag in that range moves into an anonymous body that the next version owns: version before 5 { ... } . If the range ends on the last version, a new version is created for the body. After the collapse, version 5 still sees the same data. What is gone is the ability to ask "what was version 2". Collapse is the way to say that nobody does any more. version before N is written by the Wizard. You do not write it by hand, but you may read it in a file. Note Collapse accepts a closed range: it is the way to retire history that was published once. The Example: messages that grow ends with such a collapse (step 12). Where each statement is written ¶ Statement Where Flows to tag in the root version root file every aggregate in the same and later versions tag in an aggregate version aggregate file that aggregate, later versions label any version later versions, and every aggregate when it is written in the root, see Labels ordering root file only every compile, see Ordering Tag modes ( once , local ) restrict the flow of one tag. See Tags . How a tag mode and a version mode work together is in Tag modes and version modes together .

docs.text: Benchmark ¶ examples/benchmark is a synthetic project that answers one question: how big can a project get? It builds a description of many aggregates and many versions, runs the Wizard and an XSLT over it, and measures every step. How big is a real project? ¶ Read the numbers below against two facts about real projects. Many aggregates are normal. A description with 500 aggregates (one for each message, record or data type) is an ordinary size, so the benchmark goes up to 500. Many live versions are not. Having 100 versions in use at the same time is extremely rare. A typical project keeps about 5, maybe 10. The benchmark goes to 100 to find the limit, not because a project needs it. Versions are the expensive part (see "How it grows" below), and that is a reason to retire them. When a version goes out of service, run a collapse : the old versions fold into one, and the time and the memory fall back. A project that keeps its live versions to a handful stays in the cheap corner of every table on this page. The case to look at first: 500 aggregates, 10 versions This is the size most projects will actually have, so read its numbers before the rest. Here are the rows of the static tags and no XSLT tables for it: 500 aggregates, 10 versions with your language XSLT without any XSLT 1 tag in each aggregate 76.6 s, 444 MB 44.5 s, 185 MB 100 tags in each aggregate 9 min 45 s, 2.9 GB 2 min 37 s, 1.1 GB The Wizard stays near 22 seconds in all of these rows. What grows with the tags is your XSLT and the reading of its result back: with 100 tags they are about two thirds of the run. What it does ¶ One run has a source of A aggregates (the root file, console.gal , and one file for each aggregate), each with version 0 only. Version 0 has a bit of everything: a dynamic label, a static label with tag-name-from , an important tag, a dynamic tag, a long string, an unnamed tag, a template, and the payload tags. Then the run: The Wizard batch in console.gal creates versions 1 to V-1 . Each new version rewrites the ordering of the root, deletes and creates one tag in every aggregate, and adds a new tag. create hash 0 closes version 0. xslt/suffix.xsl appends the version index to every tag string. It writes the result to intermediate/suffix-fresh.xml . The seal keeps the hashed version 0 text and moves those string changes into version 1. Galimatron compiles everything and writes the post XML. This exercises every part of the language and the run: Wizard, XSLT, seal, compilation. You can read the result in actual_gal/ and the time of each step in intermediate/galimatron.log . The machine: Intel Core i7-3770K at 3.5 GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), 32 GB of RAM, MSVC 19.51, x64, Release build with /O2 . The times are in seconds. State is how much the private memory of the process grew during the run. Dynamic tags ¶ The tag types matter. A tag with a dynamic label is copied into every new version, so T dynamic tags and V versions make T * V copies. docs.text: Configuration (gal.cfg) ¶ gal.cfg says what a run does: which folders it reads and writes, and which of your XSLT it runs. It is JSON, and it allows // comments. It is passed to Galimatron on the command line: galimatron --gal-config-file gal.cfg --log-config-file log.cfg Paths in gal.cfg are absolute, or relative to the folder of gal.cfg . This makes a project movable: copy the folder and it still runs. (Two exceptions are noted below: the XSLT file and the principal XML file have their own base folders.) The whole file ¶ { "galimatron" : { "input-gal-dir" : "incoming_gal/", "output-gal-dir" : "incoming_gal/", "intermediate-xml-dir" : "intermediate/", "intermediate-log-dir" : "intermediate/", "intermediate-summary-dir" : "intermediate/", "committed-report" : true }, "saxon-processor" : { "working-dir" : "xslt/", "config-file" : "config.xml" }, "transforms" : { "language-transforms" : { "buildin-transforms" : { }, "user-transforms" : { "transforms" : [ ... ] } }, "post-language-transforms" : { "user-transforms" : { "transforms" : [ ... ] } } } } galimatron: folders ¶ Key Meaning input-gal-dir Where the .gal files are read from, with all subfolders. output-gal-dir Where the .gal files are written back. Make it the same folder as input-gal-dir . intermediate-xml-dir The XML dumps ( lang-*.xml , post-compiled.xml ). intermediate-log-dir Where logs go. intermediate-summary-dir Where galimatron_summary.xml goes. committed-report true makes the summary, the log and error messages spell paths relative to the gal.cfg folder , and drops the memory size and the run time. Your files are rewritten in place ¶ Give input-gal-dir and output-gal-dir the same folder. This is how Galimatron is meant to be run: your .gal files are the memory of the project, so a run reads them and puts the result back into the same files. The Wizard changes them, your XSLT keep counters in them, and the next run starts from what the last one left. The new text is held in memory and written only if the whole run succeeds, and only into the files whose text changed. A run that fails leaves your .gal files exactly as they were. Two different folders The two keys may name different folders. Galimatron then reads the first, empties the second of .gal files at the start of every run, and writes each result file there at once. This exists for Galimatron's own tests, which compare the output with an expected folder. A project does not need it, and you should never point output-gal-dir at a folder that holds something you want. committed-report: output that you can commit ¶ A log with D:\work\project\... in it differs on every machine. With committed-report: true the summary, the info log and the exception texts use paths relative to gal.cfg , and omit the run time and the memory. The files then only change when the result changes, which is what you want when you keep them under version control, or compare them in a test. saxon-processor ¶ Saxon is the XSLT processor that is built into Galimatron and runs your XSLT. This section tells it where your XSLT live. Key Meaning working-dir The folder of your XSLT, the templates they load and the Saxon configuration. config-file The Saxon configuration, relative to working-dir . A minimal config.xml : <configuration edition="HE" xmlns="http://saxon.sf.net/ns/configuration"> <global lineNumbering="true"/> </configuration> lineNumbering makes an error in your XSLT name the line. The XSLT processor is SaxonC-HE. If you list no XSLT at all, the processor is not created and the run is faster (see Benchmark ). Transforms ¶ Transforms are optional: both lists may be empty. The primary output of Galimatron, post-compiled.xml , is written anyway, and you may read it with any tool. A transform is one of your XSLT programs and what it writes. language-transforms run before the .gal files are written back, post-language-transforms run on the compiled picture. Each list runs in order. See How a run works . { "name" : "next uuid for copies", "enable" : true, "user-data-for-info" : "any text, it is copied into the summary", "input" : { "principal-xsl" : { "file" : "generate-uuid.xsl", "parameters" : [ { "name" : "report_title", "value" : "Price list 11" } ] } }, "output" : { "principal-xml" : { "file" : "after-uuid.xml" }, "other-files" : [ ... ] } } Key Meaning name Shown in the log and the summary. Say what the transform does . enable false leaves the transform out of the run. The key may be absent: then it runs. user-data-for-info Free text. It appears in the summary, so a reader of the summary sees why the transform is there. input.principal-xsl.file The XSLT, relative to saxon-processor.working-dir . input.principal-xsl.parameters Parameters for <xsl:param name="..."> , all strings. output.principal-xml.file Optional. If present, the principal result of the transform is also saved there, relative to intermediate-xml-dir . output.other-files The places where <xsl:result-document> may write. The principal result ¶ The principal result of a transform is its main output. For a language transform it is the language XML, and it is the input of the next transform. Leave principal-xml empty and it stays in memory. Give it a file and you can read what that step produced. This is the cheapest debugging tool you have. For a post-language transform the principal result is also the input of the next post transform. A post transform that only writes files and wants to leave the compiled XML to the next one should copy its input through ( <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> ). A transform that does not copy it through replaces the document for the transforms after it, so put it last. The messages example lists its source generator last for this reason (see Order matters ). Parameters Galimatron adds ¶ Every transform receives these parameters, with absolute paths and / separators. Declare the ones you need with <xsl:param> . Parameter Value input_gal_dir galimatron.input-gal-dir output_gal_dir galimatron.output-gal-dir intermediate_xml_dir galimatron.intermediate-xml-dir intermediate_log_dir galimatron.intermediate-log-dir intermediate_summary_dir galimatron.intermediate-summary-dir saxon_working_dir saxon-processor.working-dir They are how an XSLT finds a state file without knowing the machine (see Custom states ). Where your XSLT may write ¶ An XSLT writes files with xsl:result-document . It does not write an absolute path. It names a store by an alias: <xsl:result-document href="@@generated-sql@@v6/schema.sql@@" method="text"> The href is @@ALIAS@@RELATIVE_PATH@@ . The ALIAS is the store-dir-string-alias of an entry in other-files : "other-files" : [ { "store-dir" : "generated_sql/", "store-dir-string-alias" : "generated-sql", "extentions" : [".sql"], "replace-escaped-form-to-original-symbols" : true, "delete-if-not-rewrited" : true } ] Galimatron replaces the alias with the folder. The result is generated_sql/v6/schema.sql . Why aliases? Safety. An XSLT cannot write outside the folders that gal.cfg names, and not with an extension you did not allow ( extentions ). A mistake in a path is refused, not executed. Portability. The XSLT holds no machine path. You move the output by changing gal.cfg . Review. One file, gal.cfg , lists every place the project writes. Key Meaning store-dir The folder of this store. store-dir-string-alias The alias that the XSLT uses. extentions Allowed extensions. A file with another one is refused. replace-escaped-form-to-original-symbols true turns < > & " ' in the written text back into < > & " ' . Use it for generated source text, where a template in XML had to escape them. delete-if-not-rewrited true (the default) removes files in this store that this run did not rewrite. The store then always mirrors the current description: a deleted aggregate takes its generated file with it. false keeps old files. The Example: messages that grow uses false for hand-edited conversions. Order matters ¶ Transforms run in the order of the list. In the messages example the dictionary generator is listed before the source generator, because the source generator replaces the compiled document. The user-data-for-info of such a transform says so. { "name" : "generate dictionary.md", "user-data-for-info" : "copies the compiled document through, so this stays before the source xslt" }

docs.text: Custom states ¶ Galimatron keeps one state for you: the .gal files. Sometimes your XSLT needs a memory of its own: "which conversions did I already write", "what was the last build number", "which names have I already put in the dictionary". That memory is a custom state . The problem ¶ An XSLT is a function. It reads its input and writes its output, and forgets. A generator needs a memory in three cases: A counter that must go on from where it stopped. A record of what it generated , so it does not overwrite a file that a person edited by hand. A list that grows : names, ids, a dictionary. Galimatron does not need a database for this, and your XSLT does not need a side channel. Your state lives in files next to your .gal files, and goes through version control with them. A state belongs to you. Galimatron does not read it, and does not check it. Your XSLT reads what the last run left, decides what is new, and writes it again. Two places for a state ¶ 1. In tags ¶ The simplest state is data. The counter in the hello project is a tag: version 0 { counter = { "1" }; } Each run, a language XSLT reads it, adds one, and Galimatron writes it back into the .gal file. Advantages: It is versioned like the rest of the data, and it shows in the history . It can be important : then a hash closes it with the version. The Wizard can create and edit it ( wizard create tag ... ). The compiled view carries it, so a post XSLT can read it without a file. The Example: messages that grow keeps its dictionary in tags too: an aggregate dictionary with one entry tag per name. docs.text: Logs and diagnostics ¶ A tool that edits your files must be able to explain itself. Galimatron leaves four kinds of evidence of every run: Evidence Where Answers the console (the terminal output) and galimatron.log log.cfg What happened, in order, and how long did it take? galimatron_summary.xml intermediate-summary-dir Which steps succeeded, and which files did each write? XML dumps intermediate-xml-dir What did the data look like after each step? the exception text the console and the log Why did the run stop? The log and log.cfg ¶ log.cfg is the configuration of the logger (Logme). It is JSON and passed with --log-config-file . { "home-directory": { "path": "." }, "flags": { "text-console": { "timestamp": "none", "signature": true, "method": false, "eol": true, "highlight": true }, "text-minimal": { "timestamp": "none", "signature": true, "method": false, "eol": true, "highlight": true, "subsystem": true } }, "channels": [ { "name": "", "flags": "text-console", "level": "info", "backends": [ { "type": "ConsoleBackend" } ] }, { "name": "file", "flags": "text-minimal", "level": "info", "backends": [ { "type": "FileBackend", "file": "intermediate/galimatron.log", "append": false } ] } ], "subsystems": { "allowed": [ "EXEC", "EXLIB", "RT" ] } // the real file lists them all } Part Meaning home-directory The base for relative file names. Run Galimatron from the project folder, or set an absolute path. flags What each line carries: a timestamp ( local or none ), the subsystem tag, the end of line. channels Where lines go. The unnamed channel is the console. A channel with a FileBackend writes a file. "append": false starts a new file on every run. level How much a channel shows. info is the usual level. Raise the detail to debug to see the work of each step. subsystems.allowed Which parts of Galimatron may write to the log. Two habits worth knowing: Use "timestamp": "none" in a project that commits its log: the file then only changes when the run changes. Keep one channel for the console and one for the file. The file keeps the whole story when the console has scrolled away. What the log says ¶ #RT-TRN begin of Galimatron #RT-TRN normal mode - unparsing will be overwrite incoming .gal #TR-TSP begin of transformation: 0, 'gal2cpp' #TR-TSP end of transformation: 0, 'gal2cpp': 0 min 0 sec, (15 ms) #TR-TSP begin of transformation: 2, 'cpp2cpp_wizard' #TR-TSP skip transformation ... #TR-TSP begin of transformation: 6, 'increment counter and write the greeting' #TR-TSP end of transformation: 6, 'increment counter and write the greeting': 0 min 0 sec, (20 ms) ... #RT-TRN all state: 30.7 MB (32231424 bytes) #RT-TRN end of Galimatron: 0 min 0 sec, (124 ms) Each transformation has a begin and an end line with its time. The user transforms carry the name that you gave them in gal.cfg , so a slow one is easy to find. The last lines say how much memory the state used and how long the run took. The benchmark is built on these lines. Subsystems ¶ A line carries the subsystem that wrote it. This list is in log.cfg . Remove a name to silence that part. Subsystem Part EXEC , EXLIB the executable, command line RT , RT-FS , RT-FSD , RT-CFG , RT-TRN , RT-SUM runtime: files, gal.cfg , the run, the summary TR translator in general TR-PAR , TR-BLD parser, builder TR-CMP compiler (the merge of versions) TR-G2S , TR-S2G , TR-S2S , TR-S2X , TR-X2S conversions between GaL, state and XML TR-HLD holder of the state TR-XSLT the XSLT processor TR-TSP the sequence of transformations TR-WIZ the Wizard The summary ¶ galimatron_summary.xml lists every step with its status and what it produced: <transformations state-bytes="32231424" status="success"> <transformation index="0" name="gal2cpp" from="build-in" status="SUCCESS" /> <transformation index="2" name="cpp2cpp_wizard" from="build-in" status="SKIPPED" /> <transformation index="6" name="increment counter and write the greeting" from="user" status="SUCCESS" /> <transformation index="9" name="cpp2gal" from="build-in" status="SUCCESS"> <produced-xml path="intermediate\lang-final.xml" /> <produced-files count="1"> <file index="0" path="incoming_gal\hello.gal" /> </produced-files> </transformation> <transformation index="14" name="write hello.html" from="user" status="SUCCESS"> <produced-files count="1"> <file index="0" path="page\hello.html" /> </produced-files> </transformation> </transformations> It is the answer to "which files did this run write?". from says whether a step is built in or yours. A failed run has status="fail" . With committed-report the paths are relative and the memory size is dropped, so the file can go into version control, and a test can compare it. XML dumps ¶ Galimatron saves the XML at the points where your XSLT take over and give back. File Taken Use it to see lang-parsed.xml after parsing and the first validation the language as it was read. lang-wizard.xml after the Wizard what the Wizard changed. This is the input of your first language XSLT. lang-xslt.xml after all language XSLT what your XSLT made. lang-final.xml after the seal and the second validation what is written back as .gal . post-compiled.xml after compilation what your post XSLT read. the file you name in principal-xml after that transform the result of one transform. lang-parsed.xml , lang-final.xml and post-compiled.xml are written on every run. lang-wizard.xml and lang-xslt.xml belong to the XSLT part of the run (the XML is handed to Saxon and read back), so a run with no language XSLT does not write them. The dumps answer the question "my XSLT gave the wrong result" in a mechanical way: compare the dump before your transform with the dump after it. Where they differ is your template. Tip To see one XSLT alone, give its principal-xml a file . Then open the file in an editor that can compare two files. Both the language XML and the compiled XML carry a <history> element: for each version, which tags were added, changed or deleted, and their values. Your XSLT can read it with gal:history(.) . The Example: messages that grow turns it into a dictionary of every tag name and the version that introduced it, and into history.html . taskflow.dot ¶ taskflow.dot is a Graphviz file. It draws the steps of the run and, inside the validation, each check as a subflow. Open it when you want to know which checks exist and in which order they depend on each other: dot -Tsvg intermediate/taskflow.dot -o taskflow.svg When a run fails ¶ Galimatron prints the exception, writes the same text to the log, and exits with a non-zero code. A real example, a hash that does not match: Exception details: domain: translator_library subdomain: translator_library::translator validation: what: HASH_DOES_NOT_MATCH what info: message: hash does not match: version 0: apple How to read it: what is the short name of the rule. The Reference lists them. message says in words what failed and where: version 0, the aggregate apple . For a syntax error, the message names the parsing rule that failed. The line comes from the file named in the text. domain and subdomain tell which part of the tool stopped: the translator, the runtime, the XSLT processor. The part below it ( Boost.LEAF diagnostic info ) is for the author of the tool. The first lines are the ones to read. An error in your XSLT is reported with the XSLT file, the line, and Saxon's message, because config.xml asks for line numbers. galimatron.crash.log ¶ Galimatron also names a crash log in intermediate-log-dir at the start of a run. On a normal run it stays empty. If Galimatron itself crashes (a fault of the tool, not of your data), the details go there. Attach it when you report the problem. A short checklist ¶ Look at the end of the output in the terminal where you started Galimatron (or in the Galimatron terminal panel of VS Code). The error is printed there. This has nothing to do with the Wizard file console.gal . Read what and message . Most errors say what to do. If the failure is in your XSLT, open the XML dump before it and the one after it. If you do not know which step ran, open galimatron_summary.xml . If you want to know why a step is slow, look at its time in galimatron.log .

docs.text: Editor support ¶ Galimatron works on files, so any editor will do. For Visual Studio Code there is an extension called GaL ( gal-syntax ). It does two things. To install it, open the Extensions view in Visual Studio Code, search for Galimatron , and press Install . Coloring ¶ A .gal file is recognized as the language GaL . The extension colors: comments ( // ... and /* ... */ ), strings, including raw strings R"(...)" and the _te mark of a template, keywords ( aggregate , version , label , wizard , create , ...), numbers, names and punctuation. The reason it matters: a .gal file is something you read often. With color, the structure of versions and the commands of the Wizard are visible at a glance, and an unclosed string stands out at once. Run Galimatron from the editor ¶ Open your project's gal.cfg and keep it the active editor. The command runs the open gal.cfg , and refuses any other file. Open the Command Palette and run Galimatron: execute . A gal.cfg with unsaved changes is saved first. The command runs galimatron --gal-config-file gal.cfg --log-config-file log.cfg with the folder of gal.cfg as the working directory. It needs log.cfg in the same folder as gal.cfg . Paths in log.cfg such as intermediate/galimatron.log are therefore relative to your project, as they should be. The run is a Visual Studio Code task. Its output goes to a dedicated terminal panel named Galimatron , which is cleared at each run, and the files that Galimatron rewrote update in the editor. A good loop is: edit a .gal file or write a Wizard command in console.gal , run Galimatron: execute , read the result. The executable ¶ When the extension starts, it looks for the installed executable and stores the path in the setting Galimatron: Executable ( galimatron.executable ). System It looks for In Windows galimatron.exe PATH , then Program Files\Galimatron\bin Linux galimatron PATH , /usr/bin , /usr/local/bin A path that already points to a file is left as it is, so you can set your own build there. If nothing is found, the extension asks whether you want to install Galimatron. Answer yes: it opens the Galimatron project on GitHub. Restart Visual Studio Code after the installation, so the executable can be found. The question is asked once, and the search runs again on the next start. If the path is still empty when you run the command, the extension asks you to choose the executable and stores it. A project to try ¶ The project galimatron_hello is made for this. Open its folder, open gal.cfg , run Galimatron: execute . If incoming_gal/hello.gal has a new counter and page/hello.html appears, the extension and the executable work. See Getting started .

docs.text: Entities ¶ GaL is a very simple, declarative language that looks like JSON, with a small set of entities on purpose. Anything else you need is built from tags. A GaL file is plain text, and all the state of a project is in such files: there are no binaries and no database, so a project lives in git like any other text. Entity What it is Belongs to How many root aggregate The top of the description. It lists the versions and orchestrates the aggregates. nothing exactly one aggregate A named group of tags. One message, one table, one setting group. the root, through versions any number, one file each version The content of an aggregate at one moment. an aggregate many tag A named piece of data. The main entity. a version many label Gives meaning to the values of a tag. a version many ordering Says which aggregates come before which. a root version many The problem each one solves ¶ Aggregate. A description with a hundred items in one file is hard to read and hard to merge. Each aggregate lives in its own file, so a change to apple is a change to apple.gal , and two people rarely edit the same file. Root aggregate. Items often share settings: a currency, a namespace, a flag that says "published". You do not want to repeat them. A tag written in the root flows into every aggregate (see Aggregates and versions ). Version. Data changes, and the old state must stay available. A version is a numbered state. The root says which versions exist, and every aggregate repeats the same indexes. Tag. The unit of data: a name and values. A tag is not typed by the language. Strings, records and arrays are enough. The meaning is yours. Label. A tag often needs more than a value: a type and a name, a default, a flag. Labels give structure to values without adding keywords to the language . A label says: the first value is the type , the second is the name . See Labels . Ordering. Files have no natural order, and generated output often needs one: a type before the types that use it. An ordering says it in the data. See Ordering . What you can do with an entity ¶ Every entity has a life: it is created, it changes, it may be deleted. GaL keeps this small and clear. Entity Create Update Delete root aggregate wizard create root aggregate wizard create version not possible, the root stays aggregate aggregate Name { ... } or wizard create aggregate wizard create version delete; in a version (history stays), or wizard delete aggregate with physically version version N { } or wizard create version by tags, and by a hash that closes it wizard delete version , wizard collapse version tag a = { ... }; a = { ... }; in a later version delete a; label label name = ...; a later statement of the same name wins not possible, a label name is final ordering ordering name = { ... }; a later statement of the same name wins not possible Two kinds of delete are worth knowing: Historical delete writes delete; or delete a; into a version. The history stays in the file. The compiled view drops what was deleted from that version on. Physical delete removes the file, or removes a version from every aggregate. It is refused while a closed version still holds the aggregate, and it only removes open versions. It is for a draft that never shipped, or for a mistake. Where entities are written ¶ An aggregate is a file. A file has two parts: The first part is the declaration : which versions exist, which are closed (a hash), which are deleted. The second part is the definitions : one block per version with the tags it writes. aggregate apple { versions { 0 = { hash = 'e3b0c442...' }; 1 = { hash = '1ee2e644...' }; 2; } } version 0 { price = { "3" }; } version 1 { field important { "int", "price" }; } version 2 { } field in version 1 is a label that the root declares (see Labels ). version 2 is open and empty. It inherits everything from 0 and 1 (see Aggregates and versions ). The root aggregate has the same shape with the word root : root aggregate shop { versions { ... } } . The root file may also hold labels and orderings. Names ¶ An aggregate or tag name is a letter followed by letters, digits and underscores: apple , hello_world , version_number . Names of aggregates must be unique, ignoring case. By convention aggregate names and file names are lowercase, so that apple.gal is never confused with Apple.gal on a system that cares about case. The name of the root aggregate does not matter to the data. The word comment and the other words of the language are reserved (see the Reference ). Strings use "..." or '...' . A raw string R"(...)" keeps every character as written. Comments are // ... and /* ... */ .

docs.text: Example: messages that grow ¶ A client and a server exchange messages. The messages change over thirteen versions of the project, and every step is a complete, building, running state, so you can see in the files what each feature of Galimatron does. The project is in the Galimatron sources, in examples/uuid_protocol . Its root aggregate is called protocol , and the snippets below show the real files. Why messages ¶ Messages are a good example because they almost always need versioning . They are added and they change, old clients stay in the field, and everything must still be understood. This is exactly the problem that versions, hashes and the Wizard solve, so messages show every feature in a setting that is easy to follow. The example generates source code, because the client and the server are programs. This is a choice of the example: the same descriptions could generate a schema, another language, or documentation, because Galimatron is not tied to any output. The problem ¶ A set of messages has a life: It starts small: hello, ok, bye. It gets new messages and new fields. Version 3 of a client talks to a server that already knows version 6. The server must understand every version a client may use, and convert old messages to the new shape. Every message has a stable uuid , and the uuid must change when the message changes. A published version must never change by accident. The types, the registration of messages, the conversions and the documentation must all agree with that. Written by hand, this is a place where two copies always drift. Described in GaL, it is one description, and the code is generated. What a step contains ¶ steps/11-substitution/ readme.txt what this step shows CMakeLists.txt builds and runs the step by_hand/ code that a person writes (handlers, cases, conversion bodies) generated/ gal.cfg the configuration log.cfg incoming_gal/ the .gal files that start the step actual_gal/ the .gal files after Galimatron ran xslt/ the XSLT and their templates generated_dto/ the source files of every published version generated_conversion/ the source files of every conversion dictionary/ dictionary.md intermediate/ log, summary, XML dumps This example is also used as a test, so it keeps incoming_gal/ and actual_gal/ apart: you can compare what a step started with and what it produced (see two different folders ). Your own project uses one folder, as in Getting started . The step reads the .gal files from the previous step and applies one Wizard batch ( console.gal ). The comment above the batch says why . The model ¶ The root aggregate is protocol . Each message is an aggregate, one file each: generated/actual_gal/ protocol.gal root: versions, published, version_namespace console.gal the Wizard command (commented out after the run) dictionary.gal an aggregate: the names used in the messages system/ hello, ok, bye, error payload/ lamp, fog, vessel, watch, enums protocol.gal declares the versions and what each one is: root aggregate protocol { versions { 0 = { hash = '27025d7a...' }; 1 = { hash = '704dd06e...' }; ... 5 = { hash = 'b099af2e...' }; 6; } } version 3 { version_number = { "4" }; version_namespace = { "v4" }; published = once important { }; } Version N of the project is version N+1 of the messages. version_namespace says in which namespace the version is generated ( v4 ). published = once important { } marks a version as published. It is once : each version states it again, so a version that is not published (the last, open one) has no such tag. important puts it into the hash. A published version is closed with a hash, and the root file keeps all of them. A message is an aggregate: aggregate lamp { versions { 0 = deleted; 1 = deleted; 2 = { hash = '...' }; ...; 6; } } version 2 { payload_message = { }; struct_name = { "lamp_t" }; uuid = need_new_uuid important { "6f1e0005-0000-4000-8000-000000000001" }; field important { "bool", "lit", "false" }; } version 3 { uuid = need_new_uuid important { "6f1e0005-0000-4000-8000-000000000002" }; field important { "int", "candela", "0" }; } The lamp appears in version 2 (the earlier versions are deleted), gains a candela field in version 3, and every version has a new uuid. The field label comes from the root. The steps ¶ Step What it adds Feature 00 no generation Four system messages, written by hand, and a session: hello, ok, bye. The messages before Galimatron. 01 empty messages The four messages are described in GaL and generated. Version 0, published , a hash. The Wizard batch, hash , the first XSLT and its templates . 02 an unpublished version A new, open version 1 and a dynamic label that asks for the next uuid. Dynamic labels , create version . 03 hello gains a text hello gets a message field. A trial version is removed and replaced. Hash after the XSLT. delete version , create label , create tag , hash and XSLT . 04 system messages The system messages move to the namespace system , marked by a tag outside the hash . Tags without important . 05 the first payload lamp , the first user message, in a folder payload/ . create aggregate ... in payload , field defaults. 06 conversions The generator writes an empty conversion from each older version into the last. Custom state in a file. 07 candela and fog The lamp gets brightness. fog appears. A new published version beside closed ones. 08 enums and a vessel Two enums, a vessel, and an ordering : an enum before the type that uses it. Ordering , a second label. 09 a watch One message carries lamp and fog. Some messages become plain types. A conversion body that generation leaves for you to write. 10 a dictionary A dictionary of every tag name, built from the data. It is a new kind of entity that Galimatron does not know. State in tags, post XSLT that writes Markdown. 11 a template string A greeting substitutes {{station}} . Template strings . 12 collapse Versions 0 to 5 collapse into version 6. Collapse . Ideas worth taking from each step ¶ Step 1: one description, many outputs. The four system messages become four small .gal files, and generate-sources.xsl writes the source files of version 1 into generated_dto/v1/ : the type, get_uuid , the declarations of the handlers and the registration. The XSLT reads the compiled XML and fills text templates (see Generating text ). Step 2: ids that move by themselves. uuid is a tag with the dynamic label need_new_uuid . A new version copies it, and the copy asks the XSLT for the next uuid: // generate-uuid.xsl <xsl:template match="tag[gal:tag-uses-dynamic(., 'need_gen_uuid')]/values/value/string/text()"> <xsl:value-of select="gal:next-uuid(.)"/> </xsl:template> The uuid has the form 6f1e0005-0000-4000-8000-000000000002 . The first groups name the message, the last group is a version counter. The result: no one types a uuid, and no one forgets to change it. Step 3: the hash covers what the XSLT made. The Wizard batch ends with create hash . The hash is taken after generate-uuid.xsl , so it includes the new uuids. The hashes of version 0 stay, because its closed values did not change. Step 4: not everything is important . system_message is a tag outside the hash. It decides the namespace in which a type is generated. Moving the system messages did not break any hash, because this change is not part of what was published. Steps 5 to 8: the messages grow. Each step is one Wizard batch: create version , new aggregates and tags, create tag protocol published = once important { } , create hash . The batch is the change request . Its comment says why. The old versions are untouched, and every hash stays true. In step 8 the batch also writes an ordering: create ordering protocol enum_precedes_struct = { sea_state_enum, fog, vessel_kind_enum, vessel }; Without it, the generated code would put fog before sea_state_enum , and the code would not compile. Steps 6 and 9: conversions. For each pair of published versions the generator writes an empty conversion, for example from version 3 to version 6: a function that takes the old message and the server state, and has an empty body. A person writes the body once (it is in by_hand/conversion/ ). The generator keeps a file that is already recorded in conversion-state.xml , so it never overwrites the work. The store has delete-if-not-rewrited: false . See Custom states . Step 10: the dictionary. The data knows every tag name and the version that introduced it (the history element). The XSLT adds an entry for each name that has none, and a person writes the text of an entry. The result is the generated dictionary.md : ## Version 2 - `lit` - `payload_message`: a user message, not a system message Important Look at what happened in this step. Galimatron has no "dictionary" and no "dictionary entry" in its model, and it was not changed to get one. The dictionary is an ordinary aggregate, dictionary , whose tags hold the entries. It has versions and a history like everything else, a person edits it like any other .gal file, and one XSLT keeps it complete while another prints it. So a new kind of thing, shaped to what this project needs, was made from the parts that every project already has: aggregates, versions, tags, and XSLT. This is the way to use the tool. The model is small on purpose, and a thing it lacks is built from it, not asked from it. Step 11: a string that quotes a tag. station = { "North Light" } and greeting = { "{{station}} on watch"_te } . The .gal file keeps {{station}} , the compiled data holds North Light on watch , and the dictionary shows it. Step 12: collapse. wizard collapse version 0-5 retires six versions into one anonymous body owned by version 6. The generator now writes only v6 , and the conversions are not generated. A client that speaks an older version gets the error no message with uuid . This is the end of life of old versions as a deliberate command. What the post XSLT write, and in what order ¶ gal.cfg of step 11 lists three post-language transforms: # Transform Writes 1 history-page.xsl intermediate/history.html , from the history element 2 generate-dictionary.xsl dictionary/dictionary.md 3 generate-sources.xsl generated_dto/ , generated_conversion/ , actual_gal/conversion-state.xml (and two language transforms before them: generate-uuid.xsl and fill-dictionary.xsl ). The sources generator is last: it does not copy the compiled document through, so the transforms that copy it must come before. Try it ¶ Open steps/11-substitution/generated/ and look at gal.cfg , xslt/ and intermediate/ . Run Galimatron there, then compare incoming_gal/ with actual_gal/ : the Wizard batch in console.gal is commented out in actual_gal/ , and the new tags are in the .gal files next to it. intermediate/galimatron.log shows the time of each step, and the dumps show the data after each one. Then read by_hand/ to see what is not generated: the handlers, the test cases and the conversion bodies. That is the border between what Galimatron owns and what a person owns.

docs.text: Getting started ¶ This page installs Galimatron and runs the smallest useful project. You will see what you write, what Galimatron changes, and what your XSLT produce. Install ¶ Galimatron is one executable ( galimatron.exe on Windows, galimatron on Linux) with the SaxonC libraries beside it (Saxon is the XSLT processor that Galimatron uses to run your XSLT). The installer puts these in place, in the install folder (on Windows, C:\Program Files\Galimatron ): What Where the executable and the Saxon libraries bin/ gal-functions.xsl : helper functions for your XSLT share/galimatron/xslt/ catalog.xml : maps the address of gal-functions.xsl to that file share/galimatron/ The catalog is why your XSLT can write <xsl:include href="https://github.com/goloveshin/galimatron/xslt/gal-functions.xsl"/> and still work without a network. Galimatron loads the catalog from the folder beside bin/ . Note A build that is not installed has no catalog. Include gal-functions.xsl by a path in that case. If you use Visual Studio Code, also install the GaL extension . It colors .gal files and runs Galimatron on an open gal.cfg . A project is a folder ¶ Galimatron has no project file in a hidden place. A project is a folder with two configuration files, your .gal files and your XSLT. docs.text: Hashes and closed versions ¶ The problem ¶ You published version 2 of a description. Programs in the field were built from it, and files that were written with it are still in use. A month later somebody "fixes" a field in version 2, and now the description and everything that was shipped disagree. Nobody notices until something breaks. A hash makes this impossible to do quietly. A hash closes a version. If the important values of a closed version change, the next run fails and says which aggregates differ. What a hash covers ¶ A hash is made of the important values only: the values of tags marked important (see Tags , which also says how to decide what is important and what is not). Each aggregate has a content hash of its important tags in that version. The root stores the combination of all of them: the aggregate hashes sorted, then combined. Left out : tag names, labels, aggregate names, file names and paths, comments, and every tag that is not important . The reason is freedom. You can rename a file, move an aggregate to another folder, add a label part, add a note. The published meaning did not change, so the hash does not either. A hash is stored in the declaration of a version: versions { 0 = { hash = '27025d7a1482f343d1f2f0bb2865d7055458e172a1ff90dd9b4cccfd4aba3035' }; 1 = { hash = '704dd06e344f8b26bf000ed10194d6f0e856afec347f962900e05a15e1df091b' }; 2; } Every aggregate that is not deleted in that version stores its own hash in its own file. The root file stores the combined one. A version with a hash on the root but not on some aggregate is an error ( HASH_MUST_BE_ON_EVERY_AGGREGATE ). Closed versions ¶ A closed version is a root version that stores a hash, and every version before it . If version 3 has a hash, versions 0, 1, 2 and 3 are closed. History does not have holes. What is closed: Its important values do not change. Any change fails the check. wizard delete version refuses it. wizard delete aggregate and wizard copy aggregate refuse an aggregate that it contains. wizard create tag and the other statement commands write into the last open version , so a closed version is never touched by accident. What is still allowed in a closed version: unimportant tags, labels, comments. They are outside the hash. Creating and removing a hash ¶ wizard create hash; // the last version wizard create hash 3; // version 3 wizard create hash 3, 4; // both wizard delete hash 3; // open version 3 again, on purpose wizard create version always adds a new open version after the closed ones. The usual rhythm is: write into the open version, check, wizard create hash to publish, wizard create version to start the next. To change a closed version, first delete its hash. This is a deliberate act: you cannot do it by accident, and you must say it with a command. force ¶ wizard create hash 3 force; wizard delete hash 3 force; Normally Galimatron checks the stored hash of every version before the Wizard runs. If a stored hash does not match because you edited by hand, the run fails, and the message names the version and the aggregates. force is for the version you name. create hash ... force stores the hash of the important tags as they are now . delete hash ... force removes a hash that does not match. Use it when you know the data is right and the hash is stale. Versions you do not name are still checked. The hash and your XSLT ¶ A hash is taken from the data after the Wizard and after your language XSLT. When create hash and an XSLT that generates values (a new uuid) run together, the hash covers the generated values. The Example: messages that grow does this at step 3. Your XSLT must not break a closed version. What if it must? For example a generator changes a type name that the closed version holds. Galimatron has an answer: the seal . After your XSLT Galimatron compares the text before and after. Where the XSLT changed a value that belongs to a closed version, it moves the change to the first open version after it , and creates that version when it does not exist. The closed version keeps its text, and its hash stays true. The effect for you: an XSLT can be written as if it edits the whole description, and history is still safe. The change shows up in the first open version, where you can see it and publish it. Why there is a seal ¶ A closed version is a promise: its text and its hash stay. A language XSLT runs on the XML of every version, so a template that rewrites a value rewrites the closed versions too. An XSLT that appends the version number to every tag string does exactly that, version 0 included. Without the seal there are two outcomes. The edit stays in the closed version, the stored hash no longer matches, and the run stops with HASH_DOES_NOT_MATCH , so nothing is written. Or every language XSLT has to skip the closed versions by itself. That is possible for a narrow job: in the messages example the XSLT that fills in uuids only touches the Wizard copies that are marked for it. It is not possible for an XSLT that walks the whole document. With the seal, such an XSLT is written once, as if there were no history. What the seal does ¶ The seal compares the text before and after your XSLT and asks the questions of the picture for each change. Most runs stop at the first or second question. A new version is added only when the change belongs to a closed version and there is no version after the last hash. Where the change lands ¶ The pictures below use one XSLT. The description has a label role_mark and a tag roles = role_mark { [ "user" ] } . The language XSLT append role adds the value "global ws" to every array that has the label role_mark : <xsl:template match="array[gal:array-has-label(., 'role_mark')]"> <xsl:copy> <xsl:apply-templates select="@* | node()"/> <value> <string>global ws</string> </value> </xsl:copy> </xsl:template> The template does not ask which version it is in. It changes the roles array everywhere, in the closed versions too: That is the input of the seal. The next picture shows what the seal does with it in three layouts of the same description. In each, the roles tag gets the new value in the first version after the last hash: No version after the hash. Version 0 is closed and the XSLT edits it. The seal puts the old text back and adds version 1 with the new value. An open version already exists. The seal puts the old text back in the closed version and writes the new value into the open one. No version is added. The tag was written before the hash. The closed version 1 has no roles of its own: it sees the one from version 0. The XSLT changes roles as version 1 sees it. The seal does not patch version 0, and it does not touch version 1. It compares the tags that the last closed version has as it sees them , and writes the difference into the first version after the hash, here a new version 2. If the XSLT edits an open version itself, that edit stays and nothing is added. If it changes nothing, no version is added. A change that the last closed version does not show is restored and not copied forward. That is the case when a later closed version has already replaced that tag. Then the validation runs again. A user XSLT does not rewrite a hash, so a hash that no longer matches fails the run, and nothing is written. What Galimatron checks about hashes ¶ Rule Error The stored hash of a version equals the one computed now. HASH_DOES_NOT_MATCH , naming the aggregates of each differing version, then a version that differs only in the root. A version with a hash has it on the root and on every live aggregate. HASH_MUST_BE_ON_EVERY_AGGREGATE , naming each declaration where it is absent. create hash and delete hash name versions that exist. WIZARD_CREATE_HASH_VERSION_MUST_EXIST , WIZARD_DELETE_HASH_VERSION_MUST_EXIST A version with no hash is not checked.

docs.text: How a run works ¶ One run of Galimatron reads your .gal files, checks them, applies a Wizard command if there is one, runs your XSLT, checks again, writes the .gal files back, and runs your post XSLT. The steps ¶ Steps 1 to 8 are the language part : they work on what you wrote. Steps 9 to 11 are the post-language part : they work on the compiled picture and write files. # Step What it does for you Name in the log 1 parse Reads every .gal file in the input folder. A syntax error stops the run here, with the file and the line. gal2cpp 2 validate Checks the whole description: one root aggregate, versions without gaps, every hash matches. cpp2cpp_validate 3 Wizard Runs the one Wizard command, if a file holds one. See The Wizard . cpp2cpp_wizard 4 to XML Turns the description into XML and hands it to Saxon, the XSLT processor that is built in. cpp2xml , xml2saxon 5 your language XSLT Zero, one or many of your transforms. Each result is the next input. They may edit the description. your names 6 from XML Reads the edited XML back. xml2cpp 7 seal and validate Keeps closed versions closed, then checks again. See Hashes . cpp2cpp_after_xslt 8 write .gal Prints the new .gal text and keeps it in memory. It is written into your files when the whole run has succeeded. cpp2gal 9 compile Merges the versions into the compiled picture. cpp2post_cpp 10 compiled XML Turns that picture into XML. post_cpp2post_xml 11 your post XSLT (optional) Zero, one or many of your transforms. They read the compiled XML and write files. The XML itself is already on disk after step 10. your names If the Wizard has no command, or you list no XSLT, those steps are skipped. The log says skip transformation . A step that fails stops the run. Read the message, fix the cause, run again. Your .gal files are rewritten in place (see Configuration ), and step 8 does not touch them yet. Galimatron keeps the new text in memory and writes it only when the whole run has succeeded , post XSLT included. A failure at any step, even in your post XSLT, leaves every .gal file as it was, and a Wizard command is still there to run again. The files that other steps write are written as soon as the step finishes: the XML dumps, and the files your XSLT produce. After a failed run some of them are new and some are older. The files that an earlier run produced and this run did not rewrite are removed only after a run that succeeded. Two views of the same data ¶ The language and the compiled picture are two different views. Language is what you write and what your language XSLT edit. Each change is stated where it happened: version 1 of apple says price = "4" , and says nothing about the currency. Compiled is what your post XSLT read. Every aggregate has the full picture of every version: the root's tags flow into the aggregates, and a value stays until a later version replaces it. Why two views? When you edit, you want the smallest possible statement. When you generate, you want the full picture and no search through older versions. See Aggregates and versions for the rules of the merge. Which XSLT should I write? ¶ You want to Use a Why change data: advance a counter, give a new id, fill a table language transform The result is written back into .gal . generate code, documents, test data post-language transform It reads the full picture and cannot damage the sources. The two kinds are described in XSLT . The primary output is XML ¶ Galimatron does not generate code, documents or any other text by itself. It has no built-in generator and no templates for any language. Its primary output is XML : the description, checked and compiled, with the history of every version. intermediate/post-compiled.xml is the compiled XML. It is written on every run, with or without XSLT. The XSLT page shows what is in it. With language XSLT, the XML of the language stages ( lang-*.xml ) is written too. The .gal files are the other output: the description itself, rewritten with the Wizard's changes. Running your XSLT inside Galimatron is optional . It is the convenient path: Saxon is built in, the XSLT may write only to folders named in gal.cfg , the language XSLT may edit the data, and the seal protects closed versions. But the XML is an ordinary file. You may leave transforms empty and read post-compiled.xml with a Python script, a program in any language, or an XSLT processor of your choice. A run with no XSLT is also the fastest (see Benchmark ). Not tied to any language ¶ Because what is made out of the XML is up to you, nothing in Galimatron is tied to a language or a format. Classes in a programming language, JSON schemas, SQL, Markdown, HTML, test data: each is a few templates away. Two projects with different targets use the same Galimatron and the same GaL. The examples in this documentation generate source code, Markdown and HTML. That is the choice of the examples, not a property of the tool. What a run reads and writes ¶ It reads: gal.cfg , log.cfg , the .gal files, your XSLT and the templates they load, and the state files that your XSLT name. It writes: the .gal files (rewritten in place), the files your XSLT write (only to folders named in gal.cfg ), and the diagnostics in the intermediate folders. Your XSLT cannot write to an arbitrary path. See aliases . A run is deterministic ¶ The same .gal files and the same XSLT give the same result. This matters for generated code in version control: a run that has nothing to change leaves no diff. Your language XSLT may change the data on every run, as the counter of the hello project does. That is your choice, and the new value is written into the .gal file, so the change is visible and versioned. An XSLT that should not move a value twice must decide from the data, as the Example: messages that grow does: it advances only the copies that a new version has just made.

Every aggregate has the full picture of every version: the root's tags flow into the aggregates, and a value stays until a later version replaces it. Why two views? When you edit, you want the smallest possible statement. When you generate, you want the full picture and no search through older versions. See Aggregates and versions for the rules of the merge.
docs.title: Two views of the same data

docs.text: You want to Use a Why change data: advance a counter, give a new id, fill a table language transform The result is written back into .gal . generate code, documents, test data post-language transform It reads the full picture and cannot damage the sources. The two kinds are described in XSLT .
docs.title: Which XSLT should I write?

docs.text: Galimatron does not generate code, documents or any other text by itself. It has no built-in generator and no templates for any language. Its primary output is XML : the description, checked and compiled, with the history of every version. intermediate/post-compiled.xml is the compiled XML. It is written on every run, with or without XSLT. The XSLT page shows what is in it. With language XSLT, the XML of the language stages ( lang-*.xml ) is written too. The .gal files are the other output: the description itself, rewritten with the Wizard's changes. Running your XSLT inside Galimatron is optional . It is the convenient path: Saxon is built in, the XSLT may write only to folders named in gal.cfg , the language XSLT may edit the data, and the seal protects closed versions. But the XML is an ordinary file. You may leave transforms empty and read post-compiled.xml with a Python script, a program in any language, or an XSLT processor of your choice. A run with no XSLT is also the fastest (see Benchmark ).
docs.title: The primary output is XML

docs.text: Because what is made out of the XML is up to you, nothing in Galimatron is tied to a language or a format. Classes in a programming language, JSON schemas, SQL, Markdown, HTML, test data: each is a few templates away. Two projects with different targets use the same Galimatron and the same GaL. The examples in this documentation generate source code, Markdown and HTML. That is the choice of the examples, not a property of the tool.
docs.title: Not tied to any language

docs.text: It reads: gal.cfg , log.cfg , the .gal files, your XSLT and the templates they load, and the state files that your XSLT name. It writes: the .gal files (rewritten in place), the files your XSLT write (only to folders named in gal.cfg ), and the diagnostics in the intermediate folders. Your XSLT cannot write to an arbitrary path. See aliases .
docs.title: What a run reads and writes

docs.text: The same .gal files and the same XSLT give the same result. This matters for generated code in version control: a run that has nothing to change leaves no diff. Your language XSLT may change the data on every run, as the counter of the hello project does. That is your choice, and the new value is written into the .gal file, so the change is visible and versioned. An XSLT that should not move a value twice must decide from the data, as the Example: messages that grow does: it advances only the copies that a new version has just made.
docs.title: A run is deterministic

docs.text: Labels ¶ A label gives meaning to a tag without adding anything to the language. There are two kinds: static and dynamic . A label is declared once, with a label statement, and used by name in front of the values of tags. Static labels: naming the values ¶ A tag is a list of values. A static label says what each position means. label field = static { type, name, default }, tag-name-from { name }; field important { "int", "price", "0" }; The label field has three parts: type , name , default . The tag lists three values, so the first is the type, the second is the name, the third is the default. In the compiled XML each value carries its part as an attribute: <tag name="price"> <values> <value index="0" field="type"><string>int</string></value> <value index="1" field="name"><string>price</string></value> <value index="2" field="default"><string>0</string></value> </values> </tag> A post XSLT can ask for a part by name, with gal:labeled-string($tag, 'field', 'type') , and need not count positions. Why it helps ¶ Without labels, a tag is price = { "int", "3", "0" } and every generator must know "the third value is the default". With a label the meaning lives in the data. Adding a fourth part later changes the label, not every generator. tag-name-from ¶ tag-name-from { name } says: the tag is called by its value labeled name . The tag above is price . You can find it with //tag[@name='price'] , and you do not type the name twice. A tag written with no name of its own must get one this way. If none of its labels has tag-name-from , the run stops. A label is still how you pick out a group of tags, named or not in the text you typed. In the language XML the labels of a tag are listed in label-refs , and gal:tags-labeled($version, 'field') returns every tag that uses field . In the compiled XML a value carries its part as an attribute, so gal:labeled-string and gal:tags-with-label find it. Two tags with the same name replace each other, so a name that comes from a value follows the same rule as any other name: a later version can write field important { "long", "price" } and the type of price changes. Note A name that comes from a value competes with a name you typed. If price = { ... } and field { "int", "price" } are both in one version, one overrides the other. Keep the names apart. Several labels in one tag ¶ A tag can have more than one label. They stack: field important { "text", "message" }; field gives meaning to the values, and important is the built-in marker that puts the values into the hash . Dynamic labels: values that must change with every version ¶ Some values must be new in every version: an identifier of a message, a counter, a build number. Doing this by hand is how people forget. label need_new_uuid = dynamic { need_gen_uuid }; A dynamic label marks tags to follow every new version . The command wizard create version copies each tag that has a dynamic label into the new version. The copy carries a marker: the value of the dynamic label, here need_gen_uuid . The original has no marker. version 0 { uuid = need_new_uuid important { "6f1e0001-...-000000000001" }; } version 1 { uuid = need_new_uuid important { "6f1e0001-...-000000000001" }; } // just copied Your language XSLT then finds the copies and gives them a new value: <xsl:template match="tag[gal:tag-uses-dynamic(., 'need_gen_uuid')]/values/value/string/text()"> <xsl:value-of select="gal:next-uuid(.)"/> </xsl:template> After the run version 1 has ...0002 . Old tags have no marker, so they keep their value. See XSLT and the step 02 of the messages example . Why dynamic labels and not a script ¶ The rule "this tag is renewed with every version" is part of the data, next to the tag. Nobody has to remember it. Only the XSLT decides how to renew. A counter, a uuid, a date: the label just says that a value is due. A tag with a dynamic label is copied into every version, so the price is memory and time. The benchmark measures it. A tag that does not change should have a static label or none. Where a label lives ¶ A label is a statement of a version. Written in the root, it is visible to every aggregate. Written in an aggregate, it is visible to that aggregate. Once stated, it stays visible in later versions. A later statement of the same name replaces the earlier one. A label cannot be deleted. delete name; of a label name is an error. A label is not part of the hash: you may add a part to a label in a closed version without breaking the hash of tags. This is how the Example: messages that grow adds the dynamic label in step 2 while versions 0 and 1 stay closed. wizard create label shop field = static { type }; adds a label for you (the first word is the aggregate).

docs.text: Ordering ¶ Files have no order. Aggregates are separate files, found by name. Generated output often needs an order anyway: a type declared before the types that use it, a base item before a derived one, a table before the tables that refer to it. An ordering says it in the data. ordering shelf = { apple, pear }, { pear, plum }; An ordering is a statement of the root aggregate. It has a name and one or more parts. A part is a chain: each name comes before the next one. From chains to positions ¶ Galimatron turns the chains into an order of all aggregates, and writes the position of each one, counting from 0. Here apple has nothing before it, so it is at position 0. pear follows apple : position 1. plum follows pear : position 2. An aggregate comes after everything that precedes it in a chain. Aggregates that the ordering does not separate keep the default order (the order of the files). An aggregate that no part names goes after the named ones. The position is written into the compiled XML. Each aggregate version carries it in an orderings element: <orderings> <ordering name="shelf" index="1"/> </orderings> Your post XSLT sort by it: <xsl:for-each select="$items"> <xsl:sort select="xs:integer(orderings/ordering[@name = 'shelf']/@index)" data-type="number"/> ... </xsl:for-each> The example with messages does exactly that: its ordering puts an enumeration before the type that uses it, so the generated code is in a valid order. Your XSLT should decide what to do with an item that no part names. The example gives such an item a very large number, so a version without the ordering stays sorted by name. What is checked ¶ An ordering must be a strict weak order : If two names get different positions, a chain must connect them. Otherwise the ordering says "A is before B" with nothing to support it, and Galimatron rejects it and names the pair. A cycle ( apple before pear before apple ) is rejected, and the message names it. Names in an ordering must be aggregates that are present in that version. wizard delete aggregate refuses to remove an aggregate that a version's ordering still names. Remove the name from the ordering first. Writing an ordering ¶ ordering shelf = { apple, pear }; in the root version, or wizard create ordering shop shelf = { apple, pear }; ( shop is the root aggregate here.) A later statement of the same ordering name in a later version replaces the earlier one. An ordering cannot be deleted. Note The benchmark rewrites the ordering of its root in every new version, with every aggregate named in it, to measure the cost.
