docs.text: Tags ¶ A tag is a piece of data: a list of values, and usually a name. The name is data too, but a special part of it, because it is the key . Galimatron uses the name to tell which tag is meant: a later version that writes the same name replaces the earlier tag, delete price; removes a tag by its name, and a generator finds a tag by it. The values have none of these powers. You may leave the name out of the text and let a label supply it (see A tag with no name of its own ). A tag that never receives a name is refused. Everything you describe is a tag. The language does not know "integer", "message" or "price". It knows names and values, and your XSLT decide what they mean. price = { "3" }; The tag price has one value, the string 3 . All values are text, even a number. Your XSLT convert it when they need a number. Values ¶ A tag has a list of values in { } . Each value is a string, a record, or an array. empty = { }; currency = { "EUR" }; two = { "int", "price" }; shape = { { "k": "v", "n": ["a", "b"] }, "plain" }; Value Written as In the compiled XML string "text" , 'text' , R"(text)" <string> record { "key": value, ... } <record> with <key> array [ value, ... ] <array> A raw string R"(...)" takes every character as it is, including quotes and new lines, so it fits a block of code or markup. R"--(...)--" allows )" inside. A tag with no name of its own ¶ A name is optional. A tag can be written with labels only: field important { "int", "price" }; This tag has no name that you typed. A label must name it from one of its values ( tag-name-from ). Here the value labeled name is price , so the tag is called price . Without that, the run stops. The reason: a generator wants a list of fields , and wants to find a field by its name. You do not want to invent a tag name for each field, and you do not want the name to be written twice. Labels in front of the values ¶ Words before the values are labels: version_number = important { "2" }; field important { "text", "message" }; important is built in. It marks the values that hashes cover. field is a label that you declared (see Labels ). A tag may have several. Important ¶ Not all data in a description is equal. Some of it other things depend on, and some of it is only yours. Important data is data that something outside the description relies on, so changing it after it was published breaks that thing. The fields of a message that other programs send and read are important: a client in the field was built with them, and files written with them are still in use. So is a version number, or an identifier that must stay stable. Unimportant data is data that lives only inside your project. The name of a structure in the generated code is a good example: it is written once in the code and nobody outside ever sees it. Rename it tomorrow and no one else notices. A note for a reader, a comment text, a name that only the code uses, a switch for a generator: all of these are unimportant. A short way to decide: ask who else depends on this value? If the answer is "a program, a file or a person outside this project", mark it important . If the answer is "only the code that this project generates", leave it unmarked. uuid = need_new_uuid important { "6f1e0001-0000-4000-8000-000000000001" }; field important { "int", "price" }; struct_name = { "PriceMessage" }; version_namespace = { "v2" }; Here uuid and the field are important: they are what is published. struct_name and version_namespace are not marked. They stay out of the hash, so they may be fixed or renamed at any time, even in a closed version, and nothing breaks. The generator writes both kinds into the same DTO. The important values become its published shape, which other programs and files depend on, and the hash guards them. The unimportant values only shape the code inside the DTO. What the mark does ¶ The label important puts the values of the tag into the hash that closes a version. That is the whole mechanism. The difference shows when a closed version is touched: Important tag Tag without important Part of the hash yes (the values) no Change in an open version allowed allowed Change in a closed version the run fails: the hash does not match allowed, the hash does not change To change something important that was already published, do not edit the closed version. Create a new version ( wizard create version ) and write the new value there. The old version stays true to what was shipped, and the new one says what is true now. Do not mark too much, or too little ¶ Too much and every small edit needs a new version, because the hash fails on each change. Mark what you publish, and nothing else. Too little and a change that breaks others goes in silently, because nothing guards it. In the messages example both kinds sit side by side. The fields and the uuid of a message are important. The mark that moves the system messages into their own namespace (step 4) is not: it only decides how the code is laid out, so moving the messages did not break a single hash. Tag modes: once and local ¶ By default a tag stays: version 1 sees what version 0 wrote. A tag mode limits where one tag lives. published = once important { }; Mode Lives in Flows from the root to the aggregates (none) its version and all later versions yes once its version only yes, in the same version local its version only no The three pictures below use the same case. The root writes the tag banner in version 1, and the pictures show where banner shows up in the root and in the aggregate apple , in versions 0, 1 and 2. A green box has the tag, a struck-out box does not. No mode. The tag stays. It appears in the version where it was written and in every later one, and it flows from the root into the aggregate. A version before it does not have it. once . The tag is for one version only. It still flows from the root into the aggregate in that version, but the next version no longer has it. This is the right mode for a fact about one version: this version is published. Written in the root, it marks every aggregate of that version and does not leak into the next one. In the Example: messages that grow every version restates published = once important { } . local . The tag is for one version, and for the file it is written in. It does not flow from the root into the aggregates, so only the root has it, and only in that version. local is for a fact about this file: a note for the person who reads the aggregate, a switch that the other aggregates must not inherit. Tag modes and version modes together ¶ A tag mode ( once , local ) belongs to one tag. A version mode ( once , local , own ) belongs to the version of an aggregate. They are two separate filters, and a tag shows up in a version only if both let it through: The version mode decides which statements may reach this version: the earlier versions of the aggregate, and the statements of the root. The tag mode decides how long the tag lives: a tag with once or local is visible only in the version where it was written, and local never flows from the root into an aggregate. The picture shows the result for one aggregate, apple , in its version 1. The columns are the version mode written before 1 . The rows are the tags and where they were written. Red is a tag that the version mode cuts off. Orange is a tag that the tag mode cuts off, whatever the version mode is. Three things follow from it: A once tag of the root flows into apple in its own version only when apple takes the root in that version. In a local or own version it does not arrive, because those versions are cut off from the root. A version mode never brings a tag back that its tag mode has ended. A once or local tag written in version 0 is gone in version 1 in all four columns. What apple writes in a version itself is always there in that version, in every version mode and for every tag mode. Deleting a tag ¶ delete price; The tag is absent from this version on. An earlier version still has it, and a later version may write it again. wizard delete tag apple price writes this for you. See The Wizard . Template strings ¶ A string followed by _te is a template. The compiled value is the string with {{name}} replaced by the value of the tag name in the same version: station = { "North Light" }; greeting = { "{{station}} on watch"_te }; The .gal file keeps {{station}} . The compiled XML holds North Light on watch . Use it for a text that quotes another value, so the value is written once. Note _te renders a string inside the data. A template for a whole generated file is another feature: see Generating text .

Generating text ¶ A post XSLT often has to write a file in some format: source code, HTML, Markdown, SQL, JSON. Writing that text with xsl:text and xsl:value-of inside the XSLT mixes two things: the logic (which aggregates, which order) and the text (the shape of a table, a class, a page). The text gets hard to read, and a change of formatting means a change of logic. The recommended way is to keep the text in an XML template and let the XSLT fill it. The text can be in any language or format. The examples below produce HTML and SQL, but a template for source code in any language, JSON or a configuration file works the same way. Galimatron does not know or care what is inside. A template file ¶ A template is a small XML file. Its text is copied as it is, and elements in the code namespace are marks that the XSLT fills in. xslt/templates/page.xml (from the galimatron_hello project): Galimatron

Counter:

is a hole. The XSLT knows the value and puts it there. A template for SQL looks the same: CREATE TABLE ( ); ALTER TABLE ADD CHECK (price > 0); You can read the generated shape directly. is a hole that the XSLT fills with a list. keeps its content only when the table has a check. The XSLT that fills it ¶ The simplest filler is short: The idea: document('templates/page.xml') loads the template. The path is relative to the XSLT folder. apply-templates walks it. Text and ordinary elements are copied. A code:* element is matched by a template of yours. The values travel as a map in a tunnel parameter, so every template down the tree can read them. A mark whose name is a value in the map is replaced. A mark that is a list (like columns ) gets a template of its own, which loops over the tags and writes the lines. gal:ctx($version, ('table-name', 'checked')) builds such a map from the tags of a version. A hyphen in the mark name is an underscore in the tag name. Why this way ¶ Readable. The template looks like the output. A person who knows SQL and not XSLT can edit it. Separate. Change the formatting in the template and leave the logic. Change the logic and leave the formatting. Checked. The template is XML, so a missing closing mark is an error when the XSLT loads it. Reusable. The same marks, the same templates, in many generators. Escaping ¶ A template is XML, so < , > and & in the output must be written as < , > and & . Set replace-escaped-form-to-original-symbols to true in the other-files entry for the generated folder, and Galimatron turns them back when it writes the file. The gal.cfg of the messages example does this for its generated source files, and leaves it false for .html and .md . Note The code namespace and the mark names are a convention used by the examples. Galimatron does not interpret them. Your XSLT decides what each mark means. Strings inside tags ¶ A string in a tag can also be a template. A string followed by _te replaces {{name}} with the value of the tag name in the same version, when the data is compiled. See Tags . Use _te for a sentence inside the data, and an XML template for a whole file.

docs.text: The Wizard ¶ The Wizard is a part of Galimatron that edits your .gal files for you. You write what you want in a few words, and Galimatron makes the same change in every file that it touches. Nothing the Wizard does is magic: every change is an ordinary edit of .gal text, and you could make it by hand. Delete the hash first, on purpose. SOURCE_IN_CLOSED_VERSION A copy would change a published version. Use continue aggregate . ORDERING_NAMES_AGGREGATE Remove the aggregate from the ordering first. XSLT ¶ Galimatron has no built-in generator, because what you generate is yours. Its primary output is XML, and XSLT is the way to turn that XML into something else inside the run. Galimatron hands the data to your XSLT 3.0 programs, run by SaxonC-HE, and takes the result back. This page is about writing those programs. Important Using XSLT here is optional . The compiled XML ( post-compiled.xml ) is written on every run. If you prefer Python or any other tool, leave transforms empty and read that file. XSLT inside Galimatron adds three things: Saxon is already there, the output is confined to the folders of gal.cfg , and a language XSLT can edit the data safely (see the seal below). And nothing here is tied to a language: your XSLT can write source code in any language, JSON, SQL, Markdown, anything. You need XSLT for two different jobs: Job Kind of transform Input Output change the data language transform the language XML the changed language XML, written back into .gal make files post-language transform the compiled XML files in the folders named by gal.cfg Each list runs in order, and the result of one transform is the input of the next. Both lists are in gal.cfg . Either list may be empty. Why XSLT ¶ The data already is a tree, and XSLT is made for trees. XSLT is declarative: "when you see this tag, write that". It fits "for every aggregate of every published version". You do not need a build of your own, a language runtime or a library. A text file is the generator. It is replaceable. Two projects with different generators use the same Galimatron. It is not a fashion. XSLT 1.0 became a W3C standard in 1999, so the language is more than 25 years old, and version 3.0 (the one Galimatron uses) dates from 2017. A generator you write today will still be readable and runnable years from now. It is a full programming language (Turing-complete), with variables, functions and recursion. Whatever you need to compute, you can compute inside the template. It is the shape of the code, not its power, that is different from other languages. What SaxonC-HE does not do ¶ Saxon comes in editions, and Galimatron carries the free one, SaxonC-HE (Home Edition). Three things from the paid editions are missing. Know them before you plan a generator: No schema awareness. Your XSLT cannot validate the XML against an XSD (no xsl:import-schema , no validation="strict" , no schema-element() ). Galimatron checks its own data itself, before and after your XSLT. A check on the data that you add yourself is written in XSLT, with xsl:if and xsl:message terminate="yes" . No streaming. The whole document is held in memory while your XSLT runs. This is fine for the sizes in the benchmark , and a reason not to dump a huge data set through one transform. No parallel execution. The edition does not spread one transform over several threads. This costs little here, because Galimatron runs the transforms of a list one after another anyway. Ordinary XSLT 3.0 (functions, maps, arrays, xsl:iterate , xsl:result-document , regular expressions) works. The first XSLT: change the data ¶ A language XSLT copies everything and changes only what it matches. <xsl:transform xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform" xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" exclude-result-prefixes="xs" version="3.0" > <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> <!-- counter = { "0" } becomes { "1" }, then { "2" }, and so on --> <xsl:template match="tag[@name='counter']/values/value/string/text()"> <xsl:value-of select="xs:integer(.) + 1"/> </xsl:template> </xsl:transform> <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> is the line to remember. Without it, everything you do not match is dropped, and the data disappears. With it, the XSLT is a patch . The language XML ¶ Galimatron writes the language as XML. These are the elements you will use: <galimatron> <language> <chunk> <!-- one .gal file --> <aggregate name="apple" index="0"> <aggregate-version-declarations> <aggregate-version-declaration index="0" status="deleted"/> <aggregate-version-declaration index="1"/> </aggregate-version-declarations> <aggregate-version-definitions> <aggregate-version-definition index="1"> <tag index="0" name="price"> <label-refs/> <values> <value index="0"><string delimiter="0">3</string></value> </values> </tag> </aggregate-version-definition> </aggregate-version-definitions> </aggregate> </chunk> </language> <history>...</history> </galimatron> Element Is root-aggregate , aggregate the aggregates, with name *-version-declaration the version list: index , status="deleted" , hash *-version-definition the body of a version, with index tag a tag, with name when it has one label-refs the labels the tag uses label a label statement values/value/string a value. Records and arrays have record and array . The simplest way to learn the shape is to open intermediate/lang-wizard.xml of your project: that is the exact input of your first language XSLT. See Logs and diagnostics . The compiled XML ¶ A post XSLT reads the merged picture. There the version definitions are complete: the root's tags are in the aggregates, and earlier versions are folded in. <galimatron> <compiled> <chunk> <aggregate name="dictionary" index="0"> <aggregate-version-definitions> <aggregate-version-definition index="6" mode="own"> <orderings> <ordering name="shelf" index="4"/> </orderings> <tag index="1" name="uuid"> <values> <value index="0" entry="name"><string>uuid</string></value> <value index="1" entry="introduced"><string>0</string></value> </values> </tag> Differences from the language XML: A value carries the part of its static label as an attribute ( entry="name" ). No label-refs . Tags are merged and deleted tags are gone. Each version definition carries its orderings (the positions, see Ordering ). Template strings ( _te ) are already rendered. The aggregates of a version are not nested under the root. Use //aggregate-version-definition[@index = 3] to find all of them. See intermediate/post-compiled.xml for the real thing. gal-functions.xsl ¶ Galimatron ships gal-functions.xsl , a library of functions for these two XMLs. Include it by its address: <xsl:include href="https://github.com/goloveshin/galimatron/xslt/gal-functions.xsl"/> An installed Galimatron maps this address to the file on disk (the catalog.xml described in Getting started ), so it needs no network. Declare xmlns:gal="https://github.com/goloveshin/galimatron" . Function Returns gal:tagvalue($version, 'name') The first string of the tag name in that version, or empty. gal:has-tag($version, 'name') Whether the version has that tag. gal:labeled-string($tag, 'label', 'part') The string of the value marked by that part of a static label. (compiled) gal:tags-with-label($version, 'label') Direct tags of a version that carry a value of that label. (compiled) gal:tags-labeled($parent, 'label') Tags that use that label. (language) gal:versions-with-tag($anchor, $index, 'name') Every aggregate version of one index that has that tag. gal:version-definition($node) The version definition that contains the node. gal:version-index($node) Its index. gal:is-open-version($definition) Whether the version is live and no later version of that aggregate exists. gal:next-statement-index($version) The next free index for a new statement in that version. gal:tag-uses-dynamic($tag, 'id') Whether the tag is a Wizard copy marked by that dynamic label. gal:next-uuid($uuid) The uuid with its last group increased by one. gal:history($anchor) The history element. gal:dictionary-entry($index, $name, $introduced, $text) A new tag for a dictionary, written in the language XML. gal:ctx($version, $names) A map of tag values for a template. Hyphens in names are underscores in tags. gal:directory-uri($path) , gal:file-uri($path) A file URI for a path, for doc() . Several of these ( next-uuid , dictionary-entry , and the helpers that find messages and enums) are written for the example with messages . The rest are general. Read the file: it is short, and a good model for functions of your own. A language XSLT with state: the next uuid ¶ This is the one from the messages example. wizard create version copies each tag with a dynamic label and marks the copy. The XSLT gives the copies a new value: <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> <!-- a Wizard copy of a tag labeled need_new_uuid. the original tag has no dynamic child --> <xsl:template match="tag[gal:tag-uses-dynamic(., 'need_gen_uuid')]/values/value/string/text()"> <xsl:value-of select="gal:next-uuid(.)"/> </xsl:template> Four lines, and every message in every new version gets a new id. See Labels . A post XSLT: a dictionary ¶ This one reads the compiled XML and writes a Markdown file with an alias (see aliases ): <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> <xsl:template match="galimatron"> <xsl:copy> <xsl:apply-templates select="@* | node()"/> </xsl:copy> <xsl:result-document href="@@dictionary@@dictionary.md@@" method="text"> <xsl:text># Dictionary

</xsl:text> <xsl:for-each-group select="//aggregate[@name = 'dictionary']//tag[values/value/@entry]" group-by="string(gal:labeled-string(., 'entry', 'introduced'))"> <xsl:sort select="xs:integer(current-grouping-key())" data-type="number"/> <xsl:text>## Version </xsl:text> <xsl:value-of select="current-grouping-key()"/> <xsl:text>

</xsl:text> <xsl:for-each select="current-group()"> <xsl:sort select="@name"/> <xsl:text>- `</xsl:text><xsl:value-of select="@name"/><xsl:text>`</xsl:text> ... </xsl:for-each> </xsl:for-each-group> </xsl:result-document> </xsl:template> The template matches the document element, copies it through (so the next transform gets the same document), and also writes a file. This is the common shape of a post transform. Your XSLT and closed versions: the seal ¶ A language XSLT may change a value in a version that a hash has closed. Galimatron does not fail, and it does not rewrite history. It moves the change to the first open version. See Hashes and closed versions . The effect for you: write the XSLT as if it edits the whole description. Published versions stay what they were, and the change shows up in the open version. Working with an XSLT ¶ Start from shallow-copy . An XSLT that forgets it destroys the document. Look at the dump. Open lang-wizard.xml or post-compiled.xml , find the element, and write the template from what you see. Test one transform at a time. Give its principal-xml a file and read the result. Parameters, not paths. Pass options with parameters in gal.cfg , and use input_gal_dir and friends for folders. Say why. name and user-data-for-info in gal.cfg are read by the next person. xsl:message shows in the console. Use it to print a progress line, like the title in the example. Keep generated text in templates. See Generating text .

(compiled) gal:tags-with-label($version, 'label') Direct tags of a version that carry a value of that label. (compiled) gal:tags-labeled($parent, 'label') Tags that use that label. (language) gal:versions-with-tag($anchor, $index, 'name') Every aggregate version of one index that has that tag. gal:version-definition($node) The version definition that contains the node. gal:version-index($node) Its index. gal:is-open-version($definition) Whether the version is live and no later version of that aggregate exists. gal:next-statement-index($version) The next free index for a new statement in that version. gal:tag-uses-dynamic($tag, 'id') Whether the tag is a Wizard copy marked by that dynamic label. gal:next-uuid($uuid) The uuid with its last group increased by one. gal:history($anchor) The history element. gal:dictionary-entry($index, $name, $introduced, $text) A new tag for a dictionary, written in the language XML. gal:ctx($version, $names) A map of tag values for a template. Hyphens in names are underscores in tags. gal:directory-uri($path) , gal:file-uri($path) A file URI for a path, for doc() . Several of these ( next-uuid , dictionary-entry , and the helpers that find messages and enums) are written for the example with messages . The rest are general. Read the file: it is short, and a good model for functions of your own.

docs.text: This is the one from the messages example. wizard create version copies each tag with a dynamic label and marks the copy. The XSLT gives the copies a new value: <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> <!-- a Wizard copy of a tag labeled need_new_uuid. the original tag has no dynamic child --> <xsl:template match="tag[gal:tag-uses-dynamic(., 'need_gen_uuid')]/values/value/string/text()"> <xsl:value-of select="gal:next-uuid(.)"/> </xsl:template> Four lines, and every message in every new version gets a new id. See Labels .

This one reads the compiled XML and writes a Markdown file with an alias (see aliases ): <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/> <xsl:template match="galimatron"> <xsl:copy> <xsl:apply-templates select="@* | node()"/> </xsl:copy> <xsl:result-document href="@@dictionary@@dictionary.md@@" method="text"> <xsl:text># Dictionary

</xsl:text> <xsl:for-each-group select="//aggregate[@name = 'dictionary']//tag[values/value/@entry]" group-by="string(gal:labeled-string(., 'entry', 'introduced'))"> <xsl:sort select="xs:integer(current-grouping-key())" data-type="number"/> <xsl:text>## Version </xsl:text> <xsl:value-of select="current-grouping-key()"/> <xsl:text>

</xsl:text> <xsl:for-each select="current-group()"> <xsl:sort select="@name"/> <xsl:text>- `</xsl:text><xsl:value-of select="@name"/><xsl:text>`</xsl:text> ... </xsl:for-each> </xsl:for-each-group> </xsl:result-document> </xsl:template> The template matches the document element, copies it through (so the next transform gets the same document), and also writes a file. This is the common shape of a post transform.

docs.text: A language XSLT may change a value in a version that a hash has closed. Galimatron does not fail, and it does not rewrite history. It moves the change to the first open version. See Hashes and closed versions . The effect for you: write the XSLT as if it edits the whole description. Published versions stay what they were, and the change shows up in the open version.
docs.title: Your XSLT and closed versions: the seal

docs.text: Start from shallow-copy . An XSLT that forgets it destroys the document. Look at the dump. Open lang-wizard.xml or post-compiled.xml , find the element, and write the template from what you see. Test one transform at a time. Give its principal-xml a file and read the result. Parameters, not paths. Pass options with parameters in gal.cfg , and use input_gal_dir and friends for folders. Say why. name and user-data-for-info in gal.cfg are read by the next person. xsl:message shows in the console. Use it to print a progress line, like the title in the example. Keep generated text in templates. See Generating text .
